rules.text: design frameworks that are both powerful and easy to use.
understand and explicitly design for a broad range of developers with different programming styles, requirements, and skill levels.
understand and design for the broad variety of programming languages.
make sure that the API design specification is the central part of the design of any feature that includes a publicly accessible API.
define top usage scenarios for each major feature area.
ensure that the scenarios correspond to an appropriate abstraction level. They should roughly correspond to the end-user use cases.
design APIs by first writing code samples for the main scenarios and then defining the object model to support the code samples.
write main scenario code samples in at least two different language families (e.g., C# and F#).
writing main scenario code samples using a dynamically typed language such as PowerShell or IronPython.
rely solely on standard design methodologies when designing the public API layer of a framework.
organize usability studies to test APIs in main scenarios.
ensure that each main feature area namespace contains only types that are used in the most common scenarios. Types used in advanced scenarios should be placed in subnamespaces.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: provide simple overloads of constructors and methods. A simple overload has a very small number of parameters, and all parameters are primitives.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: have members intended for advanced scenarios on types intended for mainline scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: require users to explicitly instantiate more than one type in the most basic scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: require that users perform any extensive initialization before they can start programming basic scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: provide good defaults for all properties and parameters (using convenience overloads), if possible.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: communicate incorrect usage of APIs using exceptions.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: ensure that APIs are intuitive and can be successfully used in basic scenarios without referring to the reference documentation.
rules.section: 2.2.3 The Principle of Self-Documenting Object Models

rules.text: provide great documentation with all APIs.
rules.section: 2.2.3 The Principle of Self-Documenting Object Models

rules.text: provide code samples illustrating how to use your most important APIs in common scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.3 The Principle of Self-Documenting Object Models

rules.text: make the discussion about identifier naming choices a significant part of specification reviews.
be afraid to use verbose identifier names when doing so makes the API self-documenting.
involving technical writers early in the design process. They can be a great resource for spotting designs with bad name choices and designs that would be difficult to explain to users.
reserving the best type names for the most commonly used types.
use exception messages to communicate framework usage mistakes to the developer.
provide strongly typed APIs if at all possible.
ensure consistency with .NET and other frameworks your users are likely to interact with.
many abstractions in mainline-scenario APIs.
using a layered framework with high-level APIs optimized for productivity, and using low-level APIs optimized for power and expressiveness.
rules.section: 2.2.4.2 Exposing Layers in the Same Namespace

rules.text: mixing low-level and high-level APIs in a single namespace if the low-level APIs are very complex (i.e., they contain many types).
rules.section: 2.2.4.2 Exposing Layers in the Same Namespace

rules.text: ensure that layers of a single feature area are well integrated. Developers should be able to start programming using one of the layers and then change their code to use the other layer without rewriting the whole application.
rules.section: 2.2.4.2 Exposing Layers in the Same Namespace

rules.text: use PascalCasing for the names of namespaces, types, members, and generic type parameters.
use camelCasing for parameter names.
capitalize both characters of two-character acronyms, except the first word of a camel-cased identifier.
capitalize only the first character of acronyms with three or more characters, except the first word of a camel-cased identifier.
capitalize any of the characters of any acronyms, whatever their length, at the beginning of a camel-cased identifier.
capitalize each word in so-called closed-form compound words.
rules.section: 3.1.3 Capitalizing Compound Words and Common Terms

rules.text: assume that all programming languages are case sensitive. They are not. Names cannot differ by case alone.
choose easily readable identifier names.
favor readability over brevity. The property name `CanScrollHorizontally` is better than `ScrollableX` (an obscure reference to the *X*-axis).
use underscores, hyphens, or any other non-alphanumeric characters.
use Hungarian notation.
using identifiers that conflict with keywords of widely used programming languages.
use only ASCII characters in identifier names.
use abbreviations or contractions as part of identifier names.
use any acronyms that are not widely accepted, and even if they are, only when necessary.
use semantically interesting names rather than language-specific keywords for type names.
use a generic CLR type name, rather than a language-specific name, in the rare cases when an identifier has no semantic meaning beyond its type.
use a common name, such as *value* or *item*, rather than repeating the type name, in the rare cases when an identifier has no semantic meaning and the type of the parameter is not important.
use a name similar to the old API when creating new versions of an existing API.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: prefer adding a suffix rather than a prefix to indicate a new version of an existing API.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: using a brand-new, but meaningful, identifier, instead of adding a suffix or a prefix.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: use a numeric suffix to indicate a new version of an existing API, particularly if the existing name of the API is the only name that makes sense (e.g., if it is an industry standard) and if adding any meaningful suffix (or changing the name) is not an appropriate option.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: use the “Ex” (or a similar) suffix for an identifier to distinguish it from an earlier version of the same API.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: use the “64” suffix when introducing versions of APIs that operate on a 64-bit integer (a long integer) instead of a 32-bit integer. You only need to take this approach when the existing 32-bit API exists; don’t do it for brand-new APIs with only a 64-bit version.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: prefix namespace names with a company name to prevent namespaces from different companies from having the same name.
use a stable, version-independent product name at the second level of a namespace name.

use organizational hierarchies as the basis for names in namespace hierarchies, because group names within corporations tend to be short-lived. Organize the hierarchy of namespaces around groups of related technologies.

use PascalCasing, and separate namespace components with periods (e.g., `Microsoft.Office.PowerPoint`). If your brand employs nontraditional casing, you should follow the casing defined by your brand, even if it deviates from normal namespace casing.
using plural namespace names where appropriate.
use the same name for a namespace and a type in that namespace.
introduce overly general type names such as `Element`, `Node`, `Log`, and `Message`.
give the same name to multiple types across namespaces within a single application model.
give types names that would conflict with any type in the core namespaces.
assign type names that would conflict with other types within a single technology.
introduce type name conflicts between types in technology namespaces and an application model namespace (unless the technology is not expected to be used with the application model).
name classes and structs with nouns or noun phrases, using PascalCasing.

publicly exposed nested types. The only exception to this guideline is if variables of the nested type need to be declared only in rare scenarios such as subclassing or other advanced customization scenarios.
